items.passage:
Text 1

How did sauropods, the enormous long-necked dinosaurs, position their heads? One influential approach articulates fossil neck vertebrae so that the joints between adjacent bones overlap maximally, producing what is termed the neutral pose of the skeleton. For Diplodocus and Apatosaurus, this reconstruction yields a neck extending almost straight forward from the shoulders. <u>Thus, these sauropods most likely held their necks roughly horizontal, feeding on low-growing plants.</u>

Text 2

Articulating sauropod vertebrae for maximal overlap may well produce a nearly straight neck. But when paleontologists Michael Taylor, Mathew Wedel, and Darren Naish reviewed X-rays of living animals—mammals, turtles, lizards, crocodiles, and birds—they found that animals habitually hold their necks raised well above the neutral pose of their skeletons. Unless sauropods differed from every living group, they too probably carried their heads high.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the underlined claim in Text 1?
options: By accepting that the neck bones fit together in a nearly straight line but arguing that the approach should be applied to more sauropod species before its results are trusted
By conceding that sauropods may have lowered their heads to feed but disputing that the approach in Text 1 shows how their neck bones fit together
By allowing that the approach in Text 1 may show how the neck bones fit together best but denying that it reveals the posture in which sauropods usually carried their necks
By granting that living animals seldom hold their necks in the neutral pose of their bones but suggesting that sauropods’ enormous size may have made them an exception
items.explanation: Text 1 moves from how the vertebrae fit together (a nearly straight neck) to a claim about how sauropods actually held their necks. The author of Text 2 grants the first step (articulating the vertebrae “may well produce a nearly straight neck”) but rejects the second, because living animals “habitually hold their necks raised well above the neutral pose of their skeletons.” So the author would accept the fit of the bones while denying that it shows the animals’ usual posture.

A.recipe: D7 half right (right concession, wrong rebuttal)
A.why_wrong: Text 2 does grant the straight fit of the bones, but its objection is that living animals do not hold their necks in that pose, not that the approach needs testing on more species.

B.recipe: D7 half right (denial where the speaker concedes)
B.why_wrong: Text 2 never discusses lowering the head to feed, and it explicitly allows that the approach may correctly show how the bones fit together; it disputes only what that fit says about posture.

D.why_wrong: Text 2 raises the possibility of sauropods being different only to set it aside (“Unless sauropods differed from every living group”); its conclusion is that they, like living animals, held their heads high.

sources.what: Taylor, Wedel and Naish 2009, Acta Palaeontologica Polonica 54(2): osteological neutral pose implies horizontal necks, but living amniotes habitually hold necks extended above it, so sauropods probably did too

items.notes: Area: natural science (paleontology). Text 1 is unattributed (the neutral-pose reconstructions of Diplodocus and Apatosaurus). The concession is about a measurement and the rebuttal about the inference from it, a different axis from 3.2 (risk) and 3.9 (reputation).

band7.why: Concede-rebut with two-part options; all three distractors are half right or reverse the concession, and the key paraphrases “habitually” as “usually carried”. Stays inside the two texts’ own claims, so not band 7 (template’s band-7 model is the same-conclusion-better-evidence form).

items.passage:
Text 1

Clorinda Matto de Turner’s 1889 novel Aves sin nido (Birds Without a Nest) was among the first Latin American novels to denounce the mistreatment of Indigenous peoples, exposing how a priest, a governor, and other officials in an Andean town exploit Indigenous households. Some critics, however, consider its conclusion a lapse: the revelation that two lovers are half siblings is, they argue, a contrivance borrowed from sentimental romance that distracts from the novel’s social criticism.

Text 2

The novel’s conclusion is admittedly improbable and indebted to the popular romances of its era. Yet the secret it uncovers is that both lovers were fathered by the same parish priest. Far from abandoning the novel’s protest, the revelation intensifies it, demonstrating that clerical abuses penetrate the most intimate relationships within the town’s families.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the critics’ view of the novel’s ending presented in Text 1?
options: By granting that the ending depends on an unlikely device drawn from popular fiction but contending that it deepens rather than departs from the novel’s critique of those who hold power in the town
By agreeing that the ending distracts from the novel’s social criticism but arguing that its appeal to readers of romances helped that criticism reach a wider audience
By acknowledging that the lovers’ shared parentage is improbable but insisting that Matto de Turner included it to mock the sentimental romances of her time
By conceding that the novel’s portrayal of the clergy is exaggerated but defending the ending as the most realistic and carefully planned part of the book
items.explanation: The critics in Text 1 call the ending a borrowed romance device that distracts from the novel’s protest. The author of Text 2 grants that the ending is “admittedly improbable and indebted to the popular romances of its era,” but argues that because the lovers’ father is a priest, the revelation “intensifies” the novel’s protest. So the author would accept the charge of implausibility while denying that the ending turns away from the novel’s criticism of the town’s powerful figures.

B.why_wrong: Text 2 rejects the idea that the ending distracts from the protest, and it says nothing about the novel reaching a wider audience.

C.recipe: D7 half right (right concession, twisted rebuttal)
C.why_wrong: Text 2 does call the ending improbable, but it says the ending is indebted to popular romances, not that it mocks them; the author’s point is about the priest, not about parody.

D.recipe: D7 half right (wrong concession and wrong rebuttal)
D.why_wrong: Text 2 never calls the portrayal of the clergy exaggerated, and it calls the ending improbable rather than realistic.

sources.what: Aves sin nido (1889): exposes priest and governor exploiting Indigenous villagers; a dreadful secret prevents the lovers’ marriage because they share the same father, a parish priest, bringing the novel’s exposure to a climax (Oxford, Torn from the Nest, description)

items.notes: Area: literature (criticism). Both texts are unattributed views; the critics’ reading and the author’s reply are general positions on the novel, not quotations. The key is the longest option (planned; the batch keeps key-longest near the official rate).

band7.why: Two-part concede-rebut shell as in band-6 officials 105ea6de and 6a1dc7c5; C keeps the true concession and swaps the purpose. The key maps closely onto Text 2’s “admittedly” and “Far from abandoning”, which keeps it at 6.

items.passage:
Text 1

Since the early 2000s, an international network of nearly 4,000 autonomous Argo floats has transformed oceanography. Each float drifts at depth, ascends every ten days while measuring temperature and salinity, and transmits its observations by satellite. Around Antarctica, however, the network has a conspicuous gap. <u>In winter, sea ice blankets immense expanses of ocean, and a float ascending beneath it cannot reach the surface to transmit its data.</u>

Text 2

Beginning in the mid-2000s, researchers attached miniature sensor tags to southern elephant seals, which forage throughout the Southern Ocean and routinely dive hundreds of meters, including beneath the winter ice. The tags record temperature and salinity profiles during each dive and relay the measurements by satellite whenever a seal surfaces to breathe through cracks or openings in the ice.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the researchers in Text 2 most likely respond to the underlined portion of Text 1?
options: They would contend that the gap in coverage is smaller than it appears, since floats can sample the ice-covered waters during the summer months.
They would claim that the seals send their measurements while swimming beneath the ice, something the floats in Text 1 are unable to do.
They would argue that measurements gathered by seals are more accurate than those gathered by floats in every part of the ocean.
They would observe that animals that regularly find their way to the surface through the ice can transmit data collected in waters that floats cannot report from.
items.explanation: The underlined portion explains the floats’ blind spot: under winter ice, a float cannot reach the air to transmit. Text 2 describes seals that dive “beneath the winter ice” and relay their data “whenever a seal surfaces to breathe through cracks or openings in the ice.” The researchers would therefore note that the seals overcome exactly the obstacle that stops the floats.

A.why_wrong: Neither text discusses summer sampling by floats; Text 2 offers a way to gather winter data under the ice, not a reason the gap is small.

B.why_wrong: Text 2 says the tags send data when a seal surfaces to breathe, not while it swims beneath the ice.

C.why_wrong: Text 2 makes no comparison of accuracy between seal and float measurements, let alone across the whole ocean.

sources.what: Charrassin et al. 2008, PNAS 105(33): sea ice prevents conventional Argo floats from surfacing to transmit data; CTD tags on southern elephant seals (2004 to 2005) gave a 30-fold increase in profiles from the sea-ice zone, transmitted by satellite when the animals surfaced

items.notes: Area: natural science (oceanography). No individual researcher named, since the seal programme is a consortium (MEOP). Replaces the earlier run’s dinosaur body-mass subject to keep the batch from three Mesozoic reptile items.

band7.why: Solution mapping with the hardest distractor (B) moving one detail (sending beneath the ice rather than at the surface), as in f3c45b4f; but the link from seals to the floats’ gap is direct, not an unstated step, so 6 rather than 7.

items.passage:
Text 1

Geologists conventionally date the carving of the Grand Canyon to the past 5 to 6 million years. Measuring helium in apatite crystals, which records when rocks cooled as overlying layers eroded, geologist Rebecca Flowers and colleagues concluded in 2012 that the western Grand Canyon had been incised to nearly its present depth by 70 million years ago. Accordingly, the canyon would be over ten times older than the longstanding consensus holds.

Text 2

Applying comparable thermochronological techniques to rocks along the canyon’s length, Karl Karlstrom and colleagues determined that its segments differ substantially in age: two middle segments were incised tens of millions of years ago, but the segments at the eastern and western extremities formed within the past 5 to 6 million years. Only then did the Colorado River integrate the older valleys into one continuous canyon.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would Karlstrom and colleagues (Text 2) most likely respond to the conclusion of Flowers and colleagues discussed in Text 1?
options: By agreeing that the western canyon was deeply cut by 70 million years ago but arguing that erosion since that time has been too slow to measure
By acknowledging that parts of the canyon may be very old but denying that the canyon as a single, connected feature is nearly that ancient
By maintaining that no part of the canyon could have been carved before the Colorado River began flowing through the region 5 to 6 million years ago
By proposing that the 70-million-year date describes the canyon’s eastern end rather than its western end, where the youngest rock layers are found
items.explanation: Flowers and colleagues conclude that the canyon is about 70 million years old. Karlstrom and colleagues found that some middle segments are indeed tens of millions of years old, but the ends, including the western end, formed only in the past 5 to 6 million years, when the river linked the older valleys “into one continuous canyon.” They would therefore allow that parts of the canyon are ancient while rejecting the idea that the canyon as a whole is.

A.why_wrong: Karlstrom’s team found that the western end formed within the past 5 to 6 million years, so they would not agree it was deeply cut 70 million years ago; neither text discusses the speed of later erosion.

C.why_wrong: Text 2 says two middle segments were carved tens of millions of years ago, before the river linked them, so it does not claim that no part predates the river.

D.why_wrong: Text 2 says both the eastern and the western ends are young, and neither text says where the youngest rock layers are.

sources.what: Karlstrom et al. 2014, Nature Geoscience: middle segments 70-50 and 25-15 Ma, end segments (Marble Canyon, Westernmost Grand Canyon) 5-6 Ma; integration of older palaeocanyons 5-6 Ma; responds to Flowers 2012 70 Ma western canyon

items.notes: Area: natural science (earth science). Flowers and Farley 2012 (Science) concluded the western Grand Canyon was carved to within a few hundred meters of modern depth by about 70 Ma; the passage says “nearly its present depth”.

fixes: “along the canyon’s entire length” to “along the canyon’s length” (Karlstrom et al. dated four of the five segments; do not state it more strongly than the source)

band7.why: Refute-by-data where the student must see that old middle segments plus young ends deny an old connected canyon; A and D reuse passage details. Text 2 refutes directly rather than changing a parameter the student must apply, so 6.

items.passage:
Text 1

Joshua Plotnik and Frans de Waal observed 26 captive Asian elephants at a camp in northern Thailand. When an elephant displayed signs of distress, such as spreading its ears or raising its tail, nearby elephants often approached it, emitted soft chirping sounds, and touched its face or mouth with their trunks—behaviors observed considerably less frequently during uneventful periods. The researchers interpret this as consolation, a response indicating empathy.

Text 2

Elephants rarely confront a threat in isolation. Whatever startles one animal, whether a barking dog or a passing vehicle, is usually perceived by others nearby as well. A bystander that hurries toward an agitated companion and reaches out with its trunk may therefore be calming itself as much as the other elephant, seeking contact because it too has been unsettled by the same disturbance.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the researchers’ interpretation in Text 1 of the bystanders’ behavior?
options: That behavior may have been prompted by the bystanders’ own unease rather than by concern for the elephant in distress.
That behavior shows that elephants are startled by sudden disturbances more easily than other animals that console one another are.
That behavior was more likely a response to the signs of distress the other elephant displayed than to any disturbance the bystanders perceived themselves.
That behavior suggests that the bystanders were imitating the distressed elephant rather than recognizing its emotional state.
items.explanation: Plotnik and de Waal take the bystanders’ approaches, chirps, and trunk contact as consolation, a sign of empathy. The author of Text 2 points out that whatever upsets one elephant usually reaches the others too, so a bystander reaching out “may therefore be calming itself,” having been “unsettled by the same disturbance.” The author would therefore say the behavior might reflect the bystanders’ own unease rather than concern for another elephant.

B.why_wrong: Text 2 says disturbances affect many elephants at once, but it never compares how easily elephants and other animals are startled.

C.recipe: D2 wrong side (reverses the speaker’s point)
C.why_wrong: This is closer to Text 1’s reading. Text 2 argues the opposite: whatever startles one elephant is “usually perceived by others nearby as well,” so the bystanders may be reacting to the disturbance themselves.

D.why_wrong: Text 2 says the bystanders may have been alarmed by the same disturbance, not that they were copying the distressed elephant.

sources.what: Plotnik and de Waal 2014, PeerJ 2:e278, “Asian elephants (Elephas maximus) reassure others in distress”: 26 captive elephants in northern Thailand; bystanders made more contact and vocalizations toward distressed animals than in control periods; framed as consolation

items.notes: Area: natural science (animal behavior). Text 2 is the author’s unattributed view; the paper itself notes that distress was usually triggered by ambiguous stimuli that bystanders may also have perceived. Replaces the earlier run’s Star Carr subject, which central_ideas_and_details w3b1_21 claimed first.

fixes: C (predators, an add-on neither text raises) replaced by a reversal of Text 2’s point that bystanders perceive the same disturbance, so a wrong option now needs Text 2 read closely (hardening toward band 6)

band7.why: After the C rewrite one distractor reverses Text 2’s point and D twists it; B remains an add-on. Model 3.12 is band 6 and alt_explanation has no band-7 officials, so a strong band 6 is the ceiling.

items.passage:
Text 1

One method for determining whether comets delivered Earth’s water compares the ratio of deuterium, a heavy isotope of hydrogen, to ordinary hydrogen in cometary water with the corresponding ratio in Earth’s oceans. In 2011, Paul Hartogh and colleagues used the Herschel Space Observatory to measure this ratio in comet Hartley 2, a member of the Jupiter family of comets, which are thought to originate in the Kuiper belt beyond Neptune. The ratio closely matched that of terrestrial seawater, unlike the ratios previously measured in comets from the more distant Oort cloud, which were approximately twice as high.

Text 2

In 2014, the Rosetta spacecraft began orbiting comet 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko, which belongs to the Jupiter family of comets. Using a mass spectrometer aboard Rosetta, Kathrin Altwegg and colleagues analyzed the comet’s water vapor directly, detecting a deuterium-to-hydrogen ratio roughly three times that of terrestrial oceans—among the highest values yet measured in the solar system.
items.stem: Based on the texts, if Hartogh and colleagues (Text 1) and Altwegg and colleagues (Text 2) were aware of the findings of both studies, they would most likely agree with which statement?
options: Comets from the Oort cloud are more likely than comets from the Kuiper belt to have supplied most of the water in Earth’s oceans.
The ratio of deuterium to hydrogen in a comet’s water rises steadily the longer the comet spends in the inner solar system.
The ratio measured in Hartley 2 cannot be assumed to be typical of comets that came from the same region of the solar system as Hartley 2 did.
Measurements taken by a spacecraft orbiting a comet are more reliable than measurements taken by a telescope at a great distance.
items.explanation: Text 1 identifies Hartley 2 as a Jupiter-family comet from the Kuiper belt with an Earth-like ratio. Text 2 reports that 67P, also a Jupiter-family comet, has a ratio about three times Earth’s. Taken together, the findings show that comets from the same family can differ widely, so neither team could treat Hartley 2’s value as representative of its group.

A.why_wrong: Text 1 says Oort cloud comets have ratios about twice Earth’s, which points away from them as the source; neither text supports this comparison.

B.why_wrong: Neither text says anything about how the ratio changes over time or with a comet’s distance from the Sun.

D.why_wrong: Text 2 notes that Rosetta analyzed the water directly, but neither text claims that one method is more reliable than the other, and both results are presented as valid.

sources.what: Altwegg et al. 2015, Science: 67P D/H (5.3 ± 0.7) × 10^-4, about three times terrestrial; Hartley 2 (Hartogh 2011) Earth-like; wide range of D/H within Jupiter-family comets

items.notes: Area: natural science (astronomy). Hartogh 2011 (Nature) used Herschel; Oort cloud comets measured earlier average about twice Earth’s ratio. The key is a joint inference neither text states, as in 3.4, and is the longest option (planned).

fixes: Text 1 now says Jupiter-family comets as a group are thought to come from the Kuiper belt (was “presumably originating” attached to Hartley 2 alone), so the key’s “same region” step rests on a stated premise for 67P too

band7.why: Joint inference neither text states (Hartley 2 not typical of its group), two steps across both texts; A and D reuse passage details. Close to band 7 (template model 3.4 is band 7) but the inference is a single contrast of two values rather than a mechanism applied to a case.

items.passage:
Text 1

Pterosaurs, the flying reptiles of the Mesozoic era, were covered in fine filaments called pycnofibers, long regarded as simple hairlike strands. In 2018, however, a team led by paleontologist Zixiao Yang reported that two pterosaur fossils from China preserve pycnofibers with tufts and branches resembling the down feathers of certain dinosaurs. The team proposed that feathers may have originated in a common ancestor of pterosaurs and dinosaurs, considerably earlier than generally thought.

Text 2

Paleontologists David Unwin and David Martill are unpersuaded. Pterosaur wings were reinforced by tough internal fibers, and as a carcass decomposes, such fibers can fray, overlap, and tangle. Branching structures like those in the Chinese fossils, they argue, could result from this degradation rather than from genuine feather anatomy—and such structures appear in only a few of the many pterosaur fossils that preserve pycnofibers.
items.stem: Which choice best describes how Text 1 and Text 2 relate to each other?
options: Text 1 describes how a long-standing view of pycnofibers was overturned by new fossils, whereas Text 2 argues that the long-standing view was mistaken from the start.
Text 1 reports a discovery made in fossils from China, whereas Text 2 attributes the branching structures in those fossils to the fibers that reinforced pterosaur wings rather than to decay.
Text 1 presents a discovery and a proposal about the origin of feathers, whereas Text 2 describes additional fossils that strengthen the case for that proposal.
Text 1 reports a finding and the evolutionary conclusion drawn from it, whereas Text 2 offers a different account of the evidence on which that conclusion rests.
items.explanation: Text 1 reports Yang’s team’s finding of branched pycnofibers and their proposal that feathers arose in a shared ancestor of pterosaurs and dinosaurs. Text 2 argues that the branching could come from decaying wing fibers rather than feather structure, which undercuts the evidence for that proposal. So Text 2 offers another explanation of the evidence behind Text 1’s conclusion.

A.why_wrong: Text 1 does describe new fossils challenging the older view, but Text 2 does not attack the older view that pycnofibers were simple strands; its doubts about branching fit that view rather than reject it.

B.why_wrong: Text 2 does point to the wing fibers, but it says the branching “could result from this degradation,” that is, from the fibers fraying as the carcass decayed, not from the fibers rather than decay.

C.why_wrong: The description of Text 1 is accurate, but Text 2 challenges the proposal rather than adding fossils that support it.

sources.what: Unwin and Martill 2020, Nature Ecology & Evolution: branched filaments in Yang et al. (2018/2019) pterosaurs are degraded internal wing-membrane fibres, not protofeathers; branching in only three of about 30 specimens

items.notes: Area: natural science (paleontology). Yang et al. published online December 2018 (Nature Ecology & Evolution 3, 2019) and offered a deep common origin as one of two possibilities, so Text 1 hedges with “may have”.

fixes: B (fossil dating, which neither text raises) replaced by a half-right twist of Text 2’s own account (wing fibers “rather than decay”), so the wrong options are no longer each killed by one fact

band7.why: S4_relate has no band-7 officials. After the B rewrite two distractors are half right (A, B) and C reverses Text 2; a strong band 6.

items.passage:
Text 1

Thomas Edison’s phonograph, unveiled in 1877, recorded sound by embossing grooves into tinfoil wrapped around a rotating cylinder; a stylus retracing those grooves could then reproduce the sound. <u>Edison’s recitation of “Mary Had a Little Lamb” on the device is frequently described as the earliest recording of a human voice.</u> Within several decades, the technology he pioneered had made recorded music a fixture of domestic life.

Text 2

In 1857, French typesetter Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville patented the phonautograph, an instrument that inscribed sound waves as undulating lines on paper coated with soot. Scott intended these tracings to be examined visually; he never imagined they could be heard. In 2008, however, a team of audio historians digitally scanned his tracings and converted them into sound, revealing a recording, made in 1860, of a voice singing the French folk song “Au clair de la lune.”
items.stem: Based on the texts, what would the author of Text 2 most likely say about the claim in the underlined sentence in Text 1?
options: It is accurate, because Scott’s phonautograph could not reproduce sound and therefore did not truly record a voice.
It overlooks evidence that a human voice was captured years before Edison’s invention, even though that recording could not be heard when it was made.
It confuses two inventions, because Scott’s device was the first to record music, whereas Edison’s was the first to record speech.
It understates Scott’s influence, because Edison designed his phonograph after studying the tracings made by Scott’s device.
items.explanation: The underlined sentence calls Edison’s 1877 recitation the earliest recording of a human voice. Text 2 describes a voice that Scott’s phonautograph traced in 1860, which researchers turned into sound in 2008, even though Scott never meant the tracings to be heard. The author of Text 2 would therefore say the claim overlooks an earlier recorded voice.

A.why_wrong: Text 2 treats the 1860 tracing as a recording of a voice, one that could later be converted into sound, so the author would not call the claim accurate.

C.why_wrong: Text 2 mentions that the 1860 voice was singing, but neither text distinguishes the first recording of music from the first recording of speech.

D.why_wrong: Neither text says that Edison studied Scott’s tracings or was influenced by Scott’s device.

sources.what: Scott de Martinville’s phonautograph (patented 1857) traced sound as soot lines; First Sounds converted the 1860 “Au clair de la lune” phonautogram to sound in 2008, earlier than Edison’s 1877 “Mary Had a Little Lamb”

items.notes: Area: arts and history (history of sound recording). The key is the longest option (planned). The playback-speed correction (the 1860 recording is a man singing slowly) is left out; the passage says only “a voice singing”.

items.passage:
Text 1

When higher-income households begin moving into a lower-income urban neighborhood, rents and property values in the area typically rise. Many critics of this process, known as gentrification, contend that <u>it forces substantial numbers of longtime residents, particularly those with the fewest financial resources, out of their neighborhoods</u>. In this view, affluent newcomers do not simply join the existing community but gradually replace it.

Text 2

Using individual credit records, Lei Ding, Jackelyn Hwang, and Eileen Divringi followed Philadelphia residents through the housing boom and bust of the 2000s. Vulnerable residents—those with low credit scores and no mortgage—were generally no more likely to leave gentrifying neighborhoods than comparable residents of nongentrifying neighborhoods were. When vulnerable residents did move, however, they were more likely to relocate to lower-income neighborhoods.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would Ding, Hwang, and Divringi (Text 2) most likely respond to the underlined claim in Text 1?
options: By agreeing that gentrification displaces many vulnerable residents but noting that most of those residents eventually find housing in more prosperous neighborhoods
By arguing that gentrification primarily drives out residents with high credit scores, who can more easily afford to relocate
By suggesting that the effects of gentrification cannot be assessed until a neighborhood has finished changing
By cautioning that gentrification may not push financially vulnerable residents out as often as the claim assumes
items.explanation: The underlined claim says gentrification forces large numbers of the poorest longtime residents out. Ding, Hwang, and Divringi found that vulnerable residents were “generally no more likely to leave gentrifying neighborhoods” than similar residents elsewhere, though those who moved tended to go to lower-income areas. They would therefore suggest that such displacement happens less often than the claim assumes.

A.why_wrong: Text 2 does not agree that many vulnerable residents are displaced, and it says those who move tend to go to lower-income neighborhoods, not more prosperous ones.

B.why_wrong: Text 2 reports only on vulnerable residents; it says nothing about residents with high credit scores being driven out.

C.why_wrong: Text 2 reports findings from a period of rapid change; it never suggests that effects can be judged only after a neighborhood stops changing.

sources.what: Ding, Hwang and Divringi 2016 (Philadelphia Fed WP 15-36/R): vulnerable residents (low credit scores, no mortgage) generally no more likely to move from gentrifying neighborhoods; when they move, more likely to move to lower-income neighborhoods

items.notes: Area: social science (urban economics). Text 1 is an unattributed critics’ view. The study covers 2002 to 2014; the passage says “the housing boom and bust of the 2000s”, the paper’s own framing.

items.passage:
Text 1

In 1998, fisheries scientist Daniel Pauly and colleagues reported that the average trophic level of global fish catches—a measure of how high in the food web the harvested species feed—had been declining since the 1950s. They attributed this trend to “fishing down marine food webs”: after depleting large, long-lived predatory fish, fleets turned progressively to smaller species and invertebrates lower in the food web.

Text 2

Trevor Essington and colleagues examined catch records from 48 large marine ecosystems and found that the average trophic level of catches had declined in 30 of them. In half of those 30, however, catches of predatory fish had not decreased; fleets had simply added new fisheries for smaller species. Only in nine did the records show predators being depleted and then replaced.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would Essington and colleagues (Text 2) most likely respond to the explanation offered by Pauly and colleagues in Text 1?
options: By suggesting that it accounts for the declining trophic level of catches in only some of the ecosystems where that decline has occurred
By rejecting the finding that the average trophic level of catches has declined, since predatory fish continued to be harvested in most of the ecosystems examined
By agreeing that fleets have shifted toward smaller species but arguing that this shift has allowed populations of predatory fish to recover
By noting that the decline in trophic level occurred mainly in ecosystems where commercial fishing began only recently
items.explanation: Pauly’s team explains the falling trophic level of catches by fleets depleting predators and then turning to smaller species. Essington’s team confirms the decline in 30 ecosystems but finds that predators were depleted and replaced in only nine; in half of the 30, fleets kept catching predators and added smaller species. They would therefore say that Pauly’s explanation fits only some of the cases.

B.why_wrong: Essington’s team confirms that the trophic level of catches declined in 30 of 48 ecosystems; they question why, not whether, it declined.

C.why_wrong: Text 2 says predator catches did not decrease in many ecosystems, but it never says predator populations recovered.

D.why_wrong: Neither text discusses when commercial fishing began in different ecosystems.

sources.what: Essington, Beaudreau and Wiedenmann 2006, PNAS 103(9): 3171-3175, “Fishing through marine food webs”: mean trophic level of catches declined in 30 of 48 large marine ecosystems; sequential addition (predator catches held steady) the most common pattern, sequential collapse in 9

items.notes: Area: natural science (marine ecology). Pauly et al. 1998 (Science) coined “fishing down marine food webs”. Replaces the earlier run’s insect-decline subject (famous topic; the meta-analysis was later corrected).

fixes: source swapped from the UW press release (which counts 21 additions against the passage’s “half”) to the paper itself (DOI); the paper’s split of the 30 declines is 15 addition, 6 unclear, 9 collapse (summary of the paper on rs.resalliance.org), which matches the passage

items.passage:
Text 1

Anthropologist Joseph Henrich has argued that a population’s size constrains the complexity of the technology it can sustain. Complex skills are learned by copying experts, and imitation is usually imperfect: in a large population, some learners will match or surpass the most skilled model, but in a small, isolated one, intricate skills tend to decline with each generation. Henrich cites Tasmania, whose inhabitants, separated from mainland Australia by rising seas, gradually abandoned technologies such as bone tools.

Text 2

In a 2013 experiment, Maxime Derex and colleagues formed groups of 2 to 16 participants who played a computer game in which each person could build either a simple virtual fishing net or a far more elaborate arrowhead, observing other members’ designs between attempts. Text 1

Tango emerged during the late 1800s in the poor waterfront neighborhoods of Buenos Aires and Montevideo, cities facing each other across the Río de la Plata. Its deepest roots lie in the region’s communities of African descent. Candombe, the drumming and dance of Afro-Argentines and Afro-Uruguayans, shaped tango’s distinctive rhythm, and the word “tango” itself was long used locally for gatherings of enslaved Africans and their descendants.

Text 2

Tango took shape in the crowded tenements of Buenos Aires and Montevideo, where hundreds of thousands of European immigrants, chiefly from Italy and Spain, settled after 1870. These newcomers contributed their own songs and instruments, and the habanera, a Spanish-Cuban dance popular in the port cities, supplied much of early tango’s rhythm. Tango is best understood as the product of these mixed immigrant districts.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
options: Tango’s rhythm came mainly from the habanera, a dance that was popular in port cities.
Tango was first performed in theaters for wealthy audiences in Buenos Aires.
Tango was brought to the Río de la Plata region by immigrants from Spain.
Tango developed in working-class neighborhoods of Buenos Aires and Montevideo in the late nineteenth century.
items.explanation: The authors disagree about tango’s main roots: Text 1 stresses African-descended communities and candombe, while Text 2 stresses European immigrants and the habanera. But both place tango’s beginnings in the poor, crowded neighborhoods of Buenos Aires and Montevideo in the late 1800s (Text 1’s “poor waterfront neighborhoods,” Text 2’s “crowded tenements” after 1870).

A.why_wrong: Only Text 2 credits the habanera; Text 1 says candombe shaped tango’s beat.

B.why_wrong: Neither text mentions theaters or wealthy audiences; both place tango in poor neighborhoods.

C.why_wrong: Both texts say tango took shape in Buenos Aires and Montevideo; Text 2 says immigrants contributed to it there, not that they brought it from Spain.

Text 1

Fingerprints were proposed as a method of identifying criminals during the 1880s, but police were initially reluctant to adopt them. In Britain, the turning point came in 1905, when brothers Alfred and Albert Stratton were convicted of a double murder in Deptford, near London, after a thumbprint on a cash box was traced to Alfred. <u>The Stratton case was the first murder investigation to be solved with fingerprint evidence</u>.

Text 2

In June 1892, two young children were discovered murdered in their home in Necochea, Argentina. Their mother, Francisca Rojas, accused a neighbor. Several days afterward, police inspector Eduardo Álvarez, trained in the fingerprint classification methods of Juan Vucetich, noticed a bloody print on a bedroom door. He removed that section of the door and compared the print with Rojas’s own fingerprints. The prints matched, and Rojas confessed.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the underlined claim in Text 1?
options: Álvarez probably learned how to compare fingerprints from British police officers.
A murder case in Argentina was solved with fingerprint evidence more than ten years before the Stratton case.
Bloody fingerprints are easier to match than prints left on objects such as cash boxes.
The Stratton brothers were convicted mainly because of evidence other than the thumbprint.
items.explanation: Text 1 claims that the 1905 Stratton case was the first murder case solved with fingerprint evidence. Text 2 describes an 1892 murder in Necochea, Argentina, that was solved when a bloody print on a door was matched to Francisca Rojas, who then confessed. The author of Text 2 would point out that fingerprints solved a murder in Argentina more than ten years before the Stratton case.

A.why_wrong: Text 2 says Álvarez was trained in the methods of Juan Vucetich, not by British police.

C.why_wrong: Neither text compares how easily different kinds of prints can be matched.

D.why_wrong: Text 2 does not discuss the Stratton case at all, and Text 1 says the thumbprint led to the conviction.

items.notes: Area: history (forensic science). The Stratton case (Deptford, 1905, thumbprint on a cash box) is the well-known British first; Text 1 overstates it as the first anywhere, as 1.4’s Text 1 does with Carracci.
